justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline assumption about the underlying asset sitting near the 290–295 range at the time of forecasting. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, adjusting only slightly upward to reflect a mild positive drift assumption and recent momentum. For the 1-week estimate, I nudged the target a bit higher to 295, acknowledging that short-term mean-reversion forces and any residual trend would likely push prices marginally higher without dramatically departing from the recent range. At the 1-month horizon, I moved to 300 as a round-number central estimate, reflecting the idea that over longer periods, a modest positive drift tends to compound, though the signal becomes much weaker relative to noise.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds with time. At 1 day, realized volatility in normal market conditions suggested a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 14–15 points, which is consistent with typical daily ranges for an asset in this price neighborhood. By one week, I widened the interval substantially to plus or minus 30 points, since multi-day paths can deviate significantly from any single-day projection as new information accumulates. At one month, the interval expands to plus or minus 60 points, acknowledging that macroeconomic releases, sentiment shifts, and technical breakouts could all materialize within that window and create compounding deviations from the starting point.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in broader market sentiment — such as a hawkish central bank surprise, a geopolitical escalation, or a credit event — could produce sharp moves well below the lower bound of the 1-month interval. Liquidity gaps during off-hours or around major data releases could also cause intraday spikes that breach even the 1-day range. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst, a short-squeeze dynamic, or unexpectedly positive macroeconomic data could propel prices above the upper bounds at any horizon.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions with relatively stable volatility, which is a simplifying assumption. Real markets exhibit fat tails, volatility clustering, and regime changes that make extreme outcomes more probable than a normal distribution would suggest. If volatility were to spike — say, due to an exogenous shock — the true confidence intervals could be meaningfully wider than what I stated, particularly at the 1-month horizon where tail risks have more time to materialize.
